To define $ \Delta S_{conf} $ we begin by comparing the adsorption of alkanes in five different zeolite structures: MFI, CHA, TON, FAU, and MOR. Depicted in Figure 2A is the relationship between the entropy of an adsorbed molecule (alkanes and permanent gases) and its gas-phase entropy, where the molecular entropy on the surface never exceeds that in the gas phase. While a significant loss in entropy occurs in all five zeolites, the absolute loss in entropy is distinct for each framework. Adsorbates in TON exhibit the largest loss in entropy upon adsorption, while FAU results in the smallest entropic losses. If the molecules were to behave as immobile adsorbates on the surface, the entropy lost upon adsorption ( $ \Delta S_{ads} $) can be approximated to be equal to three degrees of translational freedom, $ ^{3,35,36} $ which can be calculated from statistical mechanics using the Sackur–Tetrode equation $ ^{37} $

ABSTRACT: Confinement of hydrocarbons in nanoscale pockets and pores provides tunable capability for controlling molecules in catalysts, sorbents, and membranes for reaction and separation applications. While computation of the enthalpic interactions of hydrocarbons in confined spaces has improved, understanding and predicting the entropy of confined molecules remains a challenge. Here we show, using a set of nine aluminosilicate zeolite frameworks with broad variation in pore and cavity structure, that the entropy of adsorption can be predicted as a linear combination of rotational and translational entropy. The extent of entropy lost upon adsorption is predicted using only a single material descriptor, the occupiable volume ( $ V_{occ} $). Predictive capability of confined molecular entropy permits an understanding of the relation with adsorption enthalpy, the ability to computationally screen microporous materials, and an understanding of the role of confinement on the kinetics of molecules in confined spaces.

On the basis of this shape-selective feature , highly effective molecular separations and selective catalytic conversions can be achieved within zeolitic structures that are difficult to accomplish with other materials and/or techniques . $ ^ { 1-3 } $ So far, several shape-selectivity mechanisms have been elucidated and applications identified. $ ^{2-18} $ In common molecular sieving, bulky molecules adsorb preferentially over bulkier species as a result of steric constraints imposed by the zeolites' framework, e.g., linear alkane molecules compared to branched isomers. $ ^{19-23} $ Besides this common adsorption competition based on molecular bulkiness, the reverse phenomenon can also occur, i.e., competitive adsorption in favor of the bulkier species. Experiments revealed preferential adsorption of branched alkanes over their linear isomers on specific zeolites with tubular pore systems such as SAPO-5 and Mordenite. $ ^{24-28} $ Molecular simulations indicated that in such zeolites, depending on conditions, branched alkanes are preferentially adsorbed at the expense of linear isomers. $ ^{29-34} $ The present manuscript discusses the mechanisms of shape selectivity in n- and isoalkane adsorption on zeolite MCM-22. This zeolite with IZA code MWW is a relatively new synthetic material that has an unusual and quite complex pore structure. $ ^{35} $ Its framework is composed of two independent pore systems. The enthalpy and the entropy contributions to the Gibbs free energies were calculated at T = 298 K and partial pressure of 1 atm (101325 Pa). The enthalpy (H) of gas-phase pyridine and acetonitrile molecules is defined as the sum of total electronic energy ( $ E_{el} $), internal vibrational energy ( $ E_{v} $), zero-point vibrational energy (ZPVE), as well as the rotational and translational contributions to the internal energy: $ H = E_{el} + E_{v} + ZPVE + E_{R} + E_{t} $. The corresponding calculated entropies (S) includes translational, ( $ S_{t} $) vibrational, ( $ S_{v} $) and rotational ( $ S_{r} $) degrees of freedom: $ S = S_{t} + S_{v} + S_{r} $. All the considered systems are in singlet state, thus the electronic contribution to the entropy is zero. Since both adsorbed molecules are constrained in the zeolite cavity their entropy contributions in the adsorption complexes were corrected as follows: the translational and rotational degrees of freedom were reduced by 1 and 1.28 [37]. The Gibbs free energies of the zeolite support consist of only vibrational and electronic contributions. The expressions of all enthalpy and entropy contributions can be found in Ref. [38].

The first attempts to describe guest-induced flexibility in zeolites were done using molecular dynamics simulations. $ ^{79-82} $ Rigid zeolitic force fields were dynamically modified using transition state theory to include lattice flexibility, and the results obtained by these models were in good agreement with experimental data. $ ^{79-81,83,84} $ It was shown that framework flexibility in silicalite-1 (MFI-type framework) is responsible for the adsorption of large molecules such as isobutane and heptane with inflection behavior at high loadings, $ ^{80} $ while enhanced self-diffusivity at low loadings of short alkanes (i.e. methane and n-butane) was observed. $ ^{81} $ Framework flexibility is also crucial for aromatics adsorption on MFI zeolite, especially at high pressures. $ ^{84,85} $ While the use of rigid zeolitic models led to the underestimation of the aromatics adsorption in MFI zeolite by a factor of two, $ ^{84,85} $ the use of flexible models to simulate diffusion coefficients of various alkanes in silicalite-1 zeolite resulted in a convergence of experimental and theoretical values. $ ^{86} $ Recently by using in situ integrated differential phase contrast scanning transmission electron microscopy (iDPC-STEM) while adsorbing benzene molecules on MFI zeolite, Xiong et al. showed that the MFI structure goes through severe deformations giving another proof of guest-induced flexibility in zeolites (see Fig. 4). $ ^{87} $

2.4.4. Trapdoor. Traditional diﬀusion models primarily consider two types of interactions: those between guest molecules (guest–guest) and those between guest molecules and the zeolite framework (guest–host). However, when cations are present in the zeolite structure, a third interaction—involving guest molecules, the framework, and cations (guest–host-cation)—must also be accounted for. A striking example of such ternary interactions is the well-known ‘‘molecular trapdoor’’. This phenomenon, also referred to as the ‘‘gating effect’’, describes a unique molecular sieving mechanism in certain zeolites and related porous materi- als. Here, extra-framework cations function as dynamic gate- keepers at pore apertures, selectively controlling molecular diffusion to achieve highly discriminative adsorption and separation.9,147,187 To date, ‘‘trapdoor’’ has been observed in several zeolites, including RHO (DNL-6),188–190 CHA (SAPO-34, SSZ-13),147,191,192 MWF (ZSM-25),149,193 HEU (Clinoptilolite),194

With the decreasing of Si/Al ratio, the concentration of BAS and the ionic strength increase simultaneously. The turnover rates of olefin formation during cyclohexanol (CyOH) dehydration within the autoclave reactor initially increase with the local ionic strength within a micropore, and further decrease along ionic strength promotion, shown as a volcano-shaped dependence of TOFs on the ionic strength of zeolites. The local ionic environments with moderate-to-high ionic strength alter the adsorption of uncharged reactants, and stabilize surface intermediates and positively charge the transition states, which eventually increase the reaction rates. But the formation and size of the H₃O⁺(H₂O)ₙ₋₁ in the zeolite pores limit the adsorption of CyOH, e.g., size exclusion effects, and decrease reaction rates. On the other hand, the higher ionic strength results in increased excess chemical potentials of the charged transition states, which in turn raises the activation Gibbs free energies²¹⁻²⁵. Iglesia and Flaherty et al. proposed that water molecules within the specific zeolite pores can modify the free energies of liquid phase and surface species via solvation²⁶⁻²⁹, participating directly as a reactant or co-catalyst³⁰⁻³², or competitively binding to the active sites³³, thus alter the rates and selectivity of catalytic reactions by orders of magnitude. In the following appendix , we derive the entropy of adsorption in the case of infinite dilution and show how it may be related to familiar thermodynamic quantities ( cf . eq 5 ) . To begin , we define our adsorption entropy in the limit of infinite dilution via

$$ \Delta s_{\mathrm{ads}}^{\infty}=\lim_{N/V\rightarrow0}\left[\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{V,T,\mathrm{ads}}-\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial N}\right)_{V,T,\mathrm{gas}}\right] $$

$$ =S_{ads}(N=1,V,T)-S_{gas}(N=1,V,T) $$

where the subscripts “ads” and “gas” labels identify the adsorbed (confined) and gas (bulk) phases, respectively. Given the constraints of a fixed number of molecules (N), volume (V), and temperature (T), it is natural to continue working in the canonical ensemble. (As in the main text, lowercase symbols identify intensive molecular or molar properties, whereas the uppercase indicates an extensive property.) For the molecules that we examine in this work (e.g., rigid molecules with no internal degrees of freedom), the canonical partition function Q may be expressed as

$$ \begin{aligned}Q(N,V,T)&=Q_{trans}(N,V,T)Q_{rot}(N,V,T)\\&\quad\times Z(N,V,T)\end{aligned} $$

where $ Q_{trans} $ and $ Q_{rot} $ are the translational and rotational partition functions (which are unaffected by confinement) and Z is the configurational partition function. The translational and rotational partition functions are available in the usual statistical mechanics texts $ ^{44,45} $ but are ultimately unimportant for the derivation that follows.

descriptor_candidates.name: occVol_confine_ratio
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Adsorption entropy loss/R scales inversely with the fraction of molecular volume that fits into the zeolite's accessible pore volume per framework density; s_ads/s_gas decreases monotonically as this ratio drops below ~1.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Confinement restricts translational freedom; entropy loss correlates with how tightly the molecule packs into occupiable pore volume (E02: single V_occ descriptor predicts confined entropy; E01: adsorbed entropy never exceeds gas phase).
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If MAE of entropy loss/R using this ratio is not lower than a size-only baseline (e.g., log(Vol)), or the correlation with entropy loss is non-monotonic across MFI/CHA/FAU/TON/MOR-like systems, the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: shape_anisotropy_confine
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Molecular asphericity (SPAN/GeDi) modulated by the framework pore-diameter anisotropy (lsd_p/lsd_f) predicts the rotational-translational partition of entropy loss: entropy loss/R increases with this product, most strongly in one-dimensional channel systems (lsd_p/lsd_f far from 1).
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Linear molecules in tubular pores lose more rotational entropy than in cages (E01: TON largest loss, FAU smallest; E04: shape selectivity from pore-molecule geometry matching). Anisotropy ratio captures 1D channel vs 3D cage confinement geometry.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If adding this descriptor to the network does not reduce MAE of entropy loss/R versus the 14-input baseline, or if entropy loss is uncorrelated with the geometric anisotropy product for cage vs channel frameworks, the hypothesis fails.

descriptor_candidates.name: freeSurf_mobility_index
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy retention (s_ads/s_gas near 1) is maximized when the accessible surface area per unit mass is high relative to molecular surface and free aperture spacing is large; descriptor predicts a two-regime behavior: high surface-accessibility systems behave as mobile 2D adsorbates (small loss), tight-aperture systems as immobile (loss ≈ full translational entropy per Sackur–Tetrode).
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Adsorbed molecules in large-pore/high-surface frameworks retain 2D translational freedom; in tight pores they become vibrationally localized (E01: immobile-adsorbate limit equals full translational entropy loss; E05: adsorbed molecules in cavities have reduced translational/rotational contributions; E10: framework flexibility permits window passage affecting mobility).
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If the descriptor's correlation with entropy loss/R is not bimodal/monotonic in the predicted direction, or MAE of entropy loss/R does not improve over the published 14-input baseline when this nonlinear re-expression is added, the hypothesis is rejected.

descriptor_candidates.name: rot_aniso_confine_index
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: The rotational fraction of adsorption entropy loss (in units of R) increases monotonically with the molecular moment-of-inertia anisotropy (PMI3/PMI1)^0.5 multiplied by the framework aperture anisotropy (lsd_p/lsd_f); systems combining anisotropic molecules with anisotropic (channel-like) apertures lose the most rotational entropy, while near-spherical molecules in cage-like frameworks (lsd_p/lsd_f near 1) lose the least.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference from E01: TON (1D channel) shows the largest entropy loss and FAU (cage) the smallest for the same adsorbates, and the loss decomposes into translational plus rotational parts. Rotation about the long axis of an anisotropic molecule is the least hindered mode; when both molecule and pore are anisotropic, rotational freedom about other axes is quenched. The two log factors re-express the published inputs as a product of molecular and framework asymmetry without adding new information.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Adding this descriptor to the 14-input network must reduce the MAE of entropy loss/R below the current best of 0.5560 (retained round-1 descriptor). Falsified if (i) MAE does not improve, or (ii) residuals show no positive rank correlation between the descriptor and rotational entropy loss across channel frameworks (TON/MOR-like) versus cages (FAU-like).

descriptor_candidates.name: packing_confinement_index
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss/R scales with the square root of molecular volume divided by the fourth root of the total accessible pore volume per framework mass (AV*density): frameworks with high framework density and small pore volume per gram confine a given molecule more strongly, so s_ads/s_gas decreases with this index across MFI/CHA/FAU/TON/MOR-like systems, approaching the immobile-adsorbate limit (loss equal to the Sackur–Tetrode translational entropy) at the highest values.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference combining E02 (occupiable volume V_occ alone predicts confined entropy) with E01 (immobile-adsorbate limit equals full translational entropy loss). AV*density is the pore-volume-per-framework-volume fraction on the source numerical scale; dividing by it penalizes tightly packed frameworks where the free path between walls is shortest, which suppresses translational configurational volume (E09: confinement enters through the configurational partition function). Distinct from the rejected occVol_confine_ratio because it uses the framework-level AV and density rather than a per-molecule occupancy ratio and applies nonlinear compressions.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Falsified if MAE of entropy loss/R with this descriptor added does not fall below 0.5560, or if the descriptor's correlation with entropy loss/R changes sign between small (Vol < ~100 A^3) and large adsorbates — since the mechanism predicts a uniform monotonic trend regardless of adsorbate size class.

descriptor_candidates.name: window_passage_penalty
descriptor_candidates.formula: log(1 + maximum(SPAN / lsd_p, GeDi / lsd_f)) * (1 + (PBF / lsd_f) ** 2)
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Adsorption entropy loss/R grows with a window-passage penalty: molecules whose length (SPAN) or gyration-range diameter (GeDi) exceeds the largest free aperture (lsd_p) must pass through windows via framework flexure, adding an entropy cost proportional to the squared ratio of the molecular smallest bounding-sphere radius (PBF) to the free aperture spacing (lsd_f). The penalty predicts a sharp (quadratic) increase in entropy loss once the molecular dimension approaches the aperture dimension, separating freely-diffusing (small loss) from sterically gated (large loss) adsorption states.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference from E10 and E06: zeolite frameworks locally distort so molecules can pass windows somewhat smaller than their free molecular size, and framework flexibility controls adsorption of bulky molecules; passing through tight windows forces transient immobilization at the transition state, which suppresses configurational entropy (E09). E05 shows reduced translational/rotational contributions for molecules constrained in cavities. The descriptor encodes a steric gating threshold using only the given size inputs.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: Falsified if MAE of entropy loss/R does not improve below 0.5560 upon adding the descriptor, or if residuals for systems with SPAN/lsd_p clearly above 1 (window-gated regime) show entropy losses statistically indistinguishable from freely diffusing systems (SPAN/lsd_p well below 1), contradicting the predicted quadratic passage penalty.
